content: Barriers such as long waiting times, as well as policy and legal obstacles, can significantly hinder access to HIV testing services, particularly for adolescents and key populations. In many settings, the reliance on laboratory-based testing methods, especially Western blotting, creates delays in linking individuals to care. A recent systematic review has shown that testing strategies involving Western blotting result in longer turnaround times, lower rates of linkage to treatment, and higher rates of loss to follow-up compared to simpler testing methods like rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and enzyme immunoassays (EIAs). Studies have also highlighted the high opportunity costs for men attending HIV services, which contributes to lower or delayed uptake of these services. Retesting for HIV is more common among individuals tested through routine provider-initiated testing and counseling (PITC) in clinical settings or home-based HIV testing services (HTS) compared to those tested at stand-alone voluntary counseling and testing (VCT) sites. Motivations for retesting among individuals who already know their HIV-positive status include doubts about the accuracy of previous tests, changes in health status, or a desire to confirm and come to terms with their diagnosis. However, retesting is not recommended for individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART), as it can yield inaccurate results. For individuals who know their HIV status but have not initiated or have discontinued treatment, retesting can serve as an opportunity to re-engage in care, build trust with healthcare workers, and familiarize themselves with the care process. A combination of interventions is necessary to improve linkage to prevention, care, and treatment for at-risk groups, particularly key populations and men, and to reduce loss to follow-up along the testing and treatment pathway. As ART coverage increases, focused messaging on retention in care is essential. Ensuring the quality of HIV testing is as important as expanding access to testing services. Misdiagnosis of HIV status remains a challenge in resource-limited settings, often due to suboptimal testing algorithms and strategies. As of 2018, only 25% of countries had HIV testing algorithms fully compliant with WHO recommendations. Many policies fail to specify the products used in testing algorithms or the need to verify an HIV-positive diagnosis through retesting before initiating lifelong treatment. Poor-quality testing can also result from issues such as inadequate product performance, improper storage or management of supplies, clerical errors, user errors in test performance or interpretation, and poor documentation. To address these issues, quality assurance (QA) systems must function effectively and expand alongside the delivery of HIV testing services. Mathematical modeling has demonstrated that using WHO-recommended testing strategies, along with QA measures like retesting to verify positive diagnoses, is cost-effective as it prevents misdiagnosis and unnecessary initiation of costly lifelong treatment. Proactive, people-centered HIV testing initiatives and stronger efforts to implement quality HTS using WHO-recommended strategies are needed. This includes emphasizing quality improvement, promoting testing in high-burden areas and among key populations, and strategically investing in efforts to increase demand for testing services. The updated WHO guidelines on HIV testing services aim to address gaps identified in the 2015 guidelines. They provide evidence-based recommendations, operational considerations, and good practices to optimize the delivery of testing services. The guidelines emphasize the importance of integrating services, such as using HIV/syphilis dual tests in antenatal care, and ensuring accurate HIV diagnoses. They also highlight the need for strategic planning and resource allocation to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of HTS programs. The guidelines are intended for national HIV program managers, particularly those in ministries of health, as well as other stakeholders involved in the provision of HTS and integrated services. They aim to support the implementation of effective and efficient HTS as a key element of national and global HIV responses. The guidelines emphasize a public health and human rights-based approach to HTS, ensuring accessibility, acceptability, and quality of services for all individuals in need. They also stress the importance of adhering to the WHO 5 Cs—Consent, Confidentiality, Counseling, Correct test results, and Connection to care and treatment services. In summary, these guidelines aim to strengthen and expand HTS by providing comprehensive, evidence-based recommendations and operational guidance to meet the needs of diverse populations and settings. They seek to support countries in achieving and sustaining low HIV incidence by 2030 through effective and efficient testing strategies and quality assurance measures.
